**NEITHER!** Both of those are fundamental Newtonian physics myths. Per NASA NTRS 20250010956 and F = m * a, mass (12,000 kg) and inertia are 100% identical everywhere in the universe—on the Moon (0.165 g), on Mars (0.379 g), and in deep space (0 g). Stopping the same velocity in vacuum requires the EXACT SAME 1.0x braking impulse (m * dv), never less and never 100x more! What 0.165 g reduces is downward weight (W = m * g) and surface traction (F_friction = mu * m * g), meaning on the Moon astronauts and rovers can skid much easier than on Earth.

Per NASA NTRS 20220004670 (`40 kWe Deployable Fission Surface Power System`, 40 kWe Fission Surface Power System) and NTRS 20040015099 (`ESM = M + (V * L_V) + (P * L_P) + (C * L_C) + (CT * D * L_CT)`), radiative heat rejection depends on the fourth power of temperature (`T_radiator^4 - T_sink^4`). At the hotter Lunar Equator (~250-390 K daytime thermal sink), each square meter of radiator rejects less heat than at the cold Lunar South Pole (~200-230 K), forcing the 40 kWe Fission Surface Power system to use **216.2 m2** of deployable radiator area at the Equator compared to **133.4 m2** at the Pole. Because larger radiators have more physical hardware mass (`M`) and require more support structure, increasing radiator area **INCREASES** the Equivalent System Mass (ESM) thermal cooling penalty (`C * L_C`)—it never cuts cooling mass!

In NASA BVAD (NTRS 20210024855), 82 kg is the standard reference body mass of one astronaut—it is **NEVER** the mass of CO2 (which is 44 g/kg)! A single astronaut consumes 0.84 kg of O2 per day and exhales 1.00 to 1.04 kg of CO2 per day.
